rashi:a1.1: Dinara hadriana: a gold dinar struck in the coinage of Hadrian Caesar and Trajan Caesar.
rashi:a1.2: And shayfa: the name of the king. [The Davidson English renders shayfa “worn-out”; see Tosafot.]
rashi:a1.3: Which are sold for twenty-five: [twenty-five] silver dinars, in Tyrian dinars.
rashi:a1.4: Deduct a sixth from them, and these are for the redemption of the son: for he holds that the sela’im of the firstborn are sela’im of four dinars, that is, the Tyrian sela, so that five sela’im come to twenty dinars.
rashi:a1.5: They are twenty-one less a danka: deduct a sixth from twenty-four, and twenty remain; and deduct a sixth from one zuz [the twenty-fifth], and twenty-one less a danka remain.
rashi:a2.1: Rather, deduct a sixth and a zuz: but it is still twenty less a danka, for when you deduct a sixth and then deduct one more, twenty less a sixth remain.
rashi:a2.2: Rather, first deduct a zuz: and twenty-four remain; then deduct a sixth from the twenty-four, and twenty remain, and these go for the redemption of the son.
rashi:a2.3: Which are twenty matkalei by the weight of the dinar: by the weight of the Tyrian dinar, as I explained.
rashi:a2.4: Which are twenty-eight and a half and half a danka: in Arabian dinars. For of Tyrian dinars, seven make ten Arabian dinars, and fourteen make twenty. Six Tyrian remain, which make eight and a half Arabian dinars and half a danka, which is a pundeyon, since a dinar is twelve pundeyonin; only that Tyrian pundeyonin are large and Arabian ones small. Since seven Tyrian make ten Arabian, each Tyrian dinar comes to an Arabian dinar and five and one-seventh Arabian pundeyonin. Go and reckon: for seven dinars, five and one-seventh pundeyonin for each dinar comes to thirty-six extra pundeyonin, which are three dinars; so it turns out that seven are ten. Therefore seven Tyrian dinars are ten, and fourteen are twenty, and six Tyrian dinars remain. Add to each dinar five and one-seventh pundeyonin: that makes thirty-one extra pundeyonin, less a little, and that little is not counted. Make the pundeyonin into dinars: thirty-one pundeyonin are two dinars, half a dinar and a pundeyon. So it turns out that six Tyrian dinars make eight and a half Arabian dinars and half a danka. This explanation I have given is written in the books, and it was not explained to us, for the great master did not explain this whole matter, “which are twenty matkalei by the weight of the dinar, which are twenty-eight and a half and half a danka”; but I found it in a responsum of the Geonim.
rashi:a3.1: The Torah’s sela’im are three [and a third]: Tyrian dinars and a third, for they are twenty ma’a.
rashi:a4.1: But isn’t the sela of the Sanctuary…: one who consecrated his field in the Jubilee year would redeem the sowing of a ḥomer of barley for fifty sela’im. And in Torat Kohanim, about one who consecrates his field, it teaches: “According to your valuation it shall stand”: he gives forty-nine sela’im and forty-nine pundeyonin for the forty-nine years of the Jubilee. “But isn’t the sela of the Sanctuary…”, that is: why did we say forty-nine pundeyonin? Isn’t the sela of the Sanctuary forty-eight pundeyonin? It turns out that he redeems the sowing of a ḥomer of barley for fifty shekels and a pundeyon.
rashi:a5.1: This pundeyon, what is its nature? For only “fifty shekels of silver” was stated.
rashi:a5.2: A kolbon for the separate payments [leprotrot]: this pundeyon is a premium, so that a kolbon, a small coin, comes to each one separately; “leprotrot” means for each one by itself, as we say in the first chapter (above, Bekhorot 5a): “and the verse counted them only in detail.” In any case it teaches that the sela of the Sanctuary is forty-eight pundeyonin, which is four Tyrian dinars, for so we say in Kiddushin (12a): six silver ma’a are a dinar, and a ma’a is two pundeyonin; so a dinar is twelve pundeyonin and a sela forty-eight. Evidently the Torah’s sela is four dinars, which is difficult for Rava.
rashi:a6.1: And we answer: after they added to it: to the Torah’s sela they added a sixth and made it the measure of the Tyrian sela, twenty-four ma’a.
rashi:a6.2: “Shall be”: “Twenty gera shall be the shekel” implies yet another state [a larger amount]. It is written in the passage of valuations. In the portion Vayikaḥ Koraḥ it is written, “It is twenty gera,” that it may not be less.
rashi:a7.1: Rav Aḥa was a priest, and Rav Ashi sent [the redemption money] to Rav Aḥa.
rashi:a7.2: Let the Master send me a third: for I gave you too much, according to Rava, who said the Torah’s sela is three dinars and a third: for five sela’im that comes to fifteen dinars, plus the thirds, which are two dinars less a third, coming to a total of seventeen zuz less a third.
rashi:a7.3: He sent him: Rav Aḥa [sent back]: Let the Master send me three zuz, for they added to them and made them the Tyrian measure, so that five sela’im are twenty zuz.
rashi:a8.1: Litrin: a maneh, which is twenty-five sela’im.
rashi:a8.2: Kintrin: a hundred sela’im in each shekel.
rashi:a8.3: As it is written, “current with the merchant”: that wherever there are merchants, they accept it as shekels.
rashi:a8.4: And there is a place where they call their shekel kintarya: for it is as large as the measure of a centenarius; therefore he gave him centenaria.
rashi:a9.1: Because of the silver [and gold] of Jerusalem: which was in the [Temple] chamber; it is consecrated and forbidden to laymen, and when the gentiles took it, they mixed it with gold coins.
rashi:a9.2: And profane it: this implies that once robbers came, they profaned it, and it went out to non-sacred status.
rashi:a10.1: Is [Jerusalem] the majority of the world? This is said in astonishment: that because of it all the gold coins in the world should be forbidden?
rashi:a10.2: Hadriana, triana, shayfa: these were of the coinage of Jerusalem, and most of these came from Jerusalem.
tosafot:a1.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: the Hadrian dinar…: this is the gold dinar [mentioned] throughout the Talmud, which is sold for twenty-five. And he concludes: deduct a zuz, and twenty-four remain; then deduct a sixth of those twenty-four, and twenty remain for the redemption of the son, that is, five sela’im, since a sela is four dinars. And it is written in the books: “which are twenty matkalei by the weight of the dinar, which are twenty-eight zuz and a half and half a danka”; it seems to be an explanation of the Geonim, who explained the five sela’im of the son according to the coinage of their own day.
tosafot:a1.2: Dinara hadriana triana shayfa: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained hadriana as named for Hadrian Caesar and triana for Trajan Caesar, and shayfa as the name of the king. Rabbeinu Tam finds this difficult, since just below it says they wished to sequester it because of the coinage of Jerusalem, and of the coin of Jerusalem we say in HaGozel Kamma (Bava Kamma 97b): David and Solomon on one side, and Jerusalem the holy city on the other. Rabbeinu Tam says that hadriana means round, as in “hadar hudrana” (Avoda Zara 22), and turyana means large, as in teritta (Ḥullin 124a); although turyana is written with a tet and teritta with a tav, one need not be particular about that; and shayfa means that its image is worn away. However, the Kuntres’s explanation can be reconciled by distinguishing between [the coins of] the First Temple and the Second Temple, as it says in Menaḥot; and we do find Hadrian Caesar in the chapter Ein Ma’amidin (Avoda Zara 32a), and so the Arukh explains.
tosafot:a1.3: In brief: The rate here, a gold dinar for twenty-five silver ones, matches Bava Metzia 44b and is implied in Bava Kamma 36a and Shevuot 44b. Tosafot wonder how the rate changed so much, since today a measure of gold is worth at most ten of silver. Rabbeinu Tam answers that a gold dinar weighed twice as much as a silver one, not as the Kuntres [Rashi] above implies, that they are equal: Ḥullin 55b also implies that a gold dinar was of a different thickness. By weight, then, gold was worth only twelve times silver, and a midrash shows the same from Aravna’s threshing floor, fifty shekels in II Samuel 24 and six hundred in I Chronicles 21 (fifty of gold being six hundred of silver), although Zevaḥim 116b explains it otherwise (fifty from each tribe). By this reckoning a gold dinar is worth twenty-four silver ones, and Rabbeinu Tam says the twenty-fifth is the premium (hekhre’a) for changing it; that is why the Gemara says “deduct a zuz and a sixth” rather than simply “a fifth” of twenty-five. This matches the premium of half a ma’a on a half-shekel in Shekalim, since a half-shekel is two dinars, twenty-four half-ma’a; and even the opinion there that the kolbon of a half-shekel is a ma’a agrees about the premium on a gold dinar. The pundeyon of the field redemption below is called a kolbon only loosely: it merely evens out the forty-nine years, and when fifty shekels are paid at once, as in a sale, no premium applies, since a premium belongs to changing coins at the money-changer. Tosafot compare weighing meat in bulk (Bava Batra 89a), which they set aside, and the brothers and partners who give a single kolbon together (56b below), which they answer by distinguishing kinds of premium. Rabbi Yehuda bar Natan explains (Bava Metzia 44b) that the extra dinar is the premium and fee of the mint: one who brings silver for twenty-five dinars to be struck gets back only twenty-four. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: Dinara hadriana: a gold dinar of the coinage of Hadrian Caesar.
gershom:a3.1: Shayfa: that is, its image [the printed text notes that the word should read ikon, image], which is as if rubbed smooth, old.
gershom:a4.1: Deduct from them a sixth: of the twenty-five, and these are for the redemption of the son. A sixth of twenty-four is four, leaving them twenty zuz; and deduct a sixth of the fifth [the twenty-fifth dinar]: it comes to twenty-one less a sixth of one. And we hold that it is twenty zuz, no less and no more.
gershom:a5.1: Rather, deduct a sixth: of the twenty-five, twenty-one remain, and deduct from that zuz a danka: it is twenty-one less a danka. Then take a zuz out of them, and these are for the redemption of the son: it is still twenty less a danka.
gershom:a6.1: Rather, deduct a zuz: first from these twenty-five, and then deduct a sixth from twenty-four: twenty zuz remain, which are the redemption of the son.
gershom:a7.1: The Torah’s sela’im are three dinars and a third of a dinar.
gershom:a8.1: Six silver ma’a are a dinar: that makes eighteen ma’a three dinars, and a third of a dinar is two ma’a. That is “twenty gera the shekel,” which is three dinars and a third of a dinar.
gershom:a9.1: But isn’t the sela of the Sanctuary forty-eight pundeyon? That makes forty-eight pundeyonin; this pundeyon, what is its function? There in Arakhin it explains: the sowing of a ḥomer of barley at fifty shekels of silver, for the forty-nine years of the Jubilee. For each year he would give a shekel, making forty-nine shekels, and the fiftieth shekel he would divide into pundeyonin, which are forty-eight pundeyonin, so that for each year he gave a shekel and a pundeyon. And yet another pundeyon he would add to the forty-ninth shekel.
gershom:a10.1: And we asked about it: this pundeyon, what is its function? For there are only forty-eight pundeyon in a shekel; this pundeyon, where does it come from?
gershom:a11.1: A kolbon for exchanging: that is, just as they added a kolbon as a premium for breaking [a shekel] into two half-shekels, so they add this pundeyon as a premium on all those forty-nine shekels, had he weighed them out in pundeyonin. We learn from here that a sela has four dinars, and you say three and a third!
gershom:a12.1: After they added to it, it is four dinars. The verse states…
gershom:a13.1: “It is”: as it is written, “And those that are to be redeemed, from a month old shall you redeem them… it is twenty gera” (Numbers 18:16).
gershom:a14.1: Seventeen: by the reckoning of Rava, who said a sela is three dinars and a third of a dinar, the redemption of the son, which is five sela’im, comes to five times three dinars and a third, that is, seventeen zuz less a third of a dinar, for the redemption of the son. He had sent him seventeen whole ones; therefore he sent him: Let the Master send me the extra third that is on them, which I sent you too much.
gershom:a15.1: That they added to them: so that a sela has four dinars, and five sela’im come to twenty dinars; and you still owe me three dinars to complete the twenty.
gershom:a16.1: That even though it is written in the Torah unspecified: for it is written “shekel of silver,” and this shekel we do not render in Aramaic as sela’im but as “diklin of silver” [so the text], because they are centenaria, for there is a place where…
gershom:a17.1: Because of the coinage of Jerusalem: for that coin was of Jerusalem, and with it they redeemed consecrated property and tithes.
rashi:b1.1: Tyrian silver: where “shekel” is written, it is a Tyrian sela, which is four dinars, as Rabbi Yoḥanan established above; and where “shekel” is not written but only “silver,” it is a Tyrian dinar.
rashi:b1.2: Provincial silver: an eighth of Tyrian silver, and that is the Syrian istera we mentioned above [49b].
rashi:b2.1: A claim: that a person claims against his fellow: I handed you such and such.
rashi:b3.1: The judges’ oath: the one that comes because of admission to part of the claim. He swears only if the claim against him is worth two ma’a, which are a third of a dinar, even though it is written, “If a man deliver to his neighbor money.”
rashi:b4.1: There it is different: for the Merciful One juxtaposed money with vessels: [just as vessels are] two of any kind, even if they are not worth a dinar, so money is two.
rashi:b4.2: And just as money is a significant item: and a silver ma’a counts as significant; so vessels must be a significant item, and not literally anything at all.
rashi:b5.1: One who exchanges a sela: from second-tithe money, who had perutot and wishes to exchange them for silver sela’im because of the burden of the road; and there the dispute concludes: Beit Shammai say, for the whole sela, coins… In any case we learn from it that he sold the tithe for perutot, although it is written, “and you shall give it for money.”
rashi:b5.2: “Money,” “money”: he amplified. “Money” is written three times there: “and you shall turn it into money,” “and bind up the money,” and “you shall give the money”; and it amplified everything.
rashi:b6.1: Worth a peruta: and that is copper.
rashi:b6.2: [“Holy,” “holy” from tithe]: about second tithe it is written “holy”: “And all the tithe of the herd or the flock, whatever passes [under the rod, the tenth shall be holy]” (Leviticus 27:32); and about consecrated property it is written: “And when a man consecrates his house to be holy” (Leviticus 27:14).
rashi:b7.1: Then she shall go out for nothing, without money: from there we derive betrothal [with money], for we say: there is no money for this master, but there is money for another master [her father].
rashi:b8.1: Set: where there is thirty or fifty; but in all those cases we challenged from, there is no set amount.
rashi:b10.1: One who strikes [ha-toke’a]: one who strikes his fellow on his ear; that is my teacher’s explanation in Bava Kamma. And here I heard: toke’a literally, that he blew a blast from his mouth into his ear. As proof for my teacher’s explanation in Bava Kamma, I heard here: “Be not of those who strike hands” (Proverbs 22:26), who strike their palm on their fellows’ palm to become guarantors for others. And Rav Ashi [so Rashi’s text; the Gemara reads Rav Asi] teaches us: do not say he should give him a Tyrian sela, which is four zuz, but a provincial sela, which is half a zuz, an eighth of the Tyrian sela.
tosafot:b1.1: In brief: In Kiddushin (11a) the Kuntres [Rashi] explained in the name of his teachers that the dinar is the smallest Tyrian coin, and brought this for Beit Shammai’s dinar for betrothal, explained by Rav Asi’s rule. Although “twenty gera the shekel” is rendered “twenty ma’a,” the ma’a did not exist in Moses’ day; there was then a weight equal to the ma’a coined later, in Onkelos’s day. The challenge from the claim of “two silver” (ma’a, since it says shtei, not shnei) is answered there because the claim needs a significant item like the vessels, and a ma’a is significant; so the verse lowers the amount from a dinar to a ma’a. By our conclusion, “set money,” the significant item instead raises it: a ma’a is needed and a peruta is not enough. Rabbeinu Sh.Y. [apparently Rashi himself, Shlomo Yitzḥaki] objected to that explanation three times: (1) if all Torah money is a dinar, how does the juxtaposition, which comes only to teach “two,” remove it? Tosafot: a juxtaposition cannot be taken by halves, and Rav, who disagrees with Shmuel (Shevuot 39b), must say so anyway, deriving both rules from the vessels. (2) Is a needle “a significant item,” when Shevuot says “vessels came out for what they are”? Tosafot: even a needle has significance, since it can do important work. (3) Shevuot says the reverse, “just as money is significant, so vessels.” Tosafot: that is Shmuel’s view; for Rav both come from vessels, and some texts of Shmuel read as here; they add that “money” implies at least a peruta, excluding a poor vessel (Bava Metzia 47a) or one worth less than a peruta (as the Jerusalem Talmud says of two needles), and money is then compared to vessels to require a ma’a. They call Rashi’s emendation in Shevuot (“af kol” for “af kelim”) needless. Rashi’s other explanation in Kiddushin, that unspecified Torah silver is the smallest Tyrian coin, which cannot be a copper peruta, so it is set at a dinar, is challenged: by his own reading in Shevuot he should emend there too; and the Ri asks why it is set at a dinar and not at the ma’a, the smallest Tyrian coin, and why, for the claim, one would not likewise say “two dinars.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b4.1: Just as vessels are two…: in Shevuot (39b) Rashi asked: from where does Shmuel derive that “vessels came out for what they are,” when the word is needed to teach “just as vessels are two”? He answered: let it write kesafim [plural money], which implies both two and a significant item. But it is puzzling: if so, from where would “a significant item” come, for I would say [kesafim means] two perutot, as said above? One may answer: [then] it should have written kesef or ḥafatzim [objects].
tosafot:b8.1: Every set amount of money stated in the Torah is Tyrian, and of their words provincial: it is puzzling, for in HaḤovel (Bava Kamma 90a) we learned about one who strikes his fellow [on the ear]: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says a maneh, and the Gemara concludes that this is a Tyrian maneh. And in Ketubot, chapter Af al pi (64b), we learned, “he gives them vessels worth fifty zuz,” and in Metziat HaIsha (67a), “he should not give her less than fifty zuz,” and the Gemara infers that it means fifty plain zuz, without inferring at all from Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi. And the ketuba of a virgin is two hundred Tyrian [zuz], whether it is from the Torah or rabbinic, and even the ketuba of a widow, which all agree is rabbinic, is a Tyrian maneh. The Ri says that here it speaks only of sela’im, like the set money stated in the Torah, where only shekels are written.
gershom:b1.1: Provincial silver: it is one-eighth of the silver of the Torah.
gershom:b2.1: The claim: on which one becomes liable to an oath when claiming “two silver,” and we hold [it means] two silver ma’a; so how can you say Tyrian silver?
gershom:b3.1: And just as money is a significant item: and two silver ma’a are also a significant item.
gershom:b4.1: One who exchanges a sela of second tithe: that if he has second-tithe coins worth sela’im and wants to exchange them for a sela. Evidently second tithe was redeemed onto [small] coins, even though it is written of it, “and you shall give it for money.”
gershom:b5.1: Then she shall go out for nothing, without money: but there is money for another master; and who is that? The father, who is entitled to his daughter’s betrothal money. And we learned: Beit Shammai… Shall we say that Rav Asi, who said Tyrian silver, holds like Beit Shammai, who say a dinar?
gershom:b6.1: Set: such as the five sela’im of the son, the thirty of the slave, and all the others.
gershom:b7.1: Rather, a sela is half a zuz, for people call half a zuz an istera, which is a sela; and this sela is one-eighth of the Torah’s sela.
